common_name: Ace Forage Cowpea (Small-Seeded Texas Wildlife and Cover Crop Cowpea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast into warm soil from mid-spring through early summer once frost danger has passed and soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Ace is a small-seeded forage cowpea bred by the Texas A&M AgriLife Research Forage Legume Breeding Program specifically for wildlife plots, cover cropping, and legume hay, released in 2018. Its smaller seed gives more seed per pound than older varieties like Iron and Clay, allowing lower seeding rates while still producing heavy biomass on sandy, low-rainfall soils. It blooms later in the season than comparable varieties, reaching first flower in late summer with seed maturing by mid-fall, which helps it avoid early frost kill in more northern parts of its range. Left to mature, a portion of its seed germinates quickly after ripening while the remainder germinates over the following months, giving stands some ability to reseed themselves.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension
Texas Department of Agriculture State Seed and Plant Board

common_name: Horizon Buckwheat (Large-Seeded Manitoba Cover Crop Buckwheat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into warm, frost-free soil any time after the last spring frost through mid-summer for a fast-smothering short-season cover.

directions: Horizon is a large-seeded buckwheat licensed in Manitoba in 2011 as an improvement on the older Mancan and Manor cultivars, offering higher grain yield and heavier test weight while keeping the same rapid weed-smothering growth habit. Broadcast seed shallowly into a warm, well-prepared seedbed after the soil has warmed, since it germinates within days and canopies quickly enough to outcompete emerging weeds. Its larger seed size means slightly heavier seeding rates than fine-seeded types are unnecessary, as bigger seedlings establish vigorously on their own. Mow or incorporate at first flower for peak biomass, since the crop is frost-tender and will volunteer readily from any seed left to mature.

common_name: Tyrone Forage Soybean (Tall Late-Season Deer and Hay Soybean)

planting.note: Drill into warm soil in late spring to early summer once frost risk has passed, giving this late-maturing type a full season to build height before fall frost.

directions: Tyrone is an exceptionally tall, indeterminate maturity-group-VII forage soybean developed by a USDA breeder and adapted to forage and grazing use across the southern states. Its late maturity and rapid vegetative growth let it keep producing palatable, high-protein browse late into the season, making it a favorite for deer food plots as well as cattle and dairy forage where herbicide-free management matters. Sow into warm, fertile soil after all frost danger has passed, since the tall vines need the full growing season to reach their height and continue setting leaf well after typical grain soybeans have begun to senesce. Moderate resistance to lodging and to Phytophthora root rot lets it hold up under repeated grazing or clipping through the summer.

common_name: Melrose Austrian Winter Pea (Ascochyta-Tolerant Winter-Hardy Forage Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early to mid-fall so vines establish before hard freezes; Melrose overwinters as a low rosette and resumes vigorous vining growth in spring.

directions: Melrose is a purple-flowered, indeterminate Austrian winter pea that ranks among the most winter-hardy field pea cultivars evaluated in southeastern variety trials, holding its own alongside Granger and Commonwinter through hard winters. Its long, sprawling vines produce heavier dry-matter yields than the older common Austrian winter and Fenn types, and it carries useful tolerance to Ascochyta blight, a common foliar disease of overwintering peas. Drill seed into a firm, fertile fall seedbed at a depth that ensures good soil contact, since the large seeds need consistent moisture to establish before cold weather sets in. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it pairs well in mixes with cereal rye or oats, using the grass as a trellis for its climbing tendrils while it fixes nitrogen for the following cash crop.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

common_name: Purple Prosperity Hairy Vetch (Early-Flowering Organic No-Till Hairy Vetch)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed in early fall so plants establish before winter; Purple Prosperity flowers earlier than common hairy vetch, timing well with roller-crimper termination ahead of a no-till cash crop.

directions: Purple Prosperity was bred jointly by USDA-ARS, the Rodale Institute, and agricultural experiment stations at Penn State and Cornell between 1998 and 2005 to combine early flowering with reliable winter survival for organic no-till systems in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic. It matched or exceeded the winter hardiness of the earlier southern-bred AU Early Cover across a decade of multi-state trials, a rare combination since early-flowering vetches often sacrifice cold tolerance. Sow inoculated seed into a well-prepared fall seedbed, ideally mixed with a cereal grain that gives the sprawling vines something to climb. Because it reaches full bloom notably earlier than standard hairy vetch, it can be terminated with a roller-crimper and no-till planted into soon enough to fit an earlier warm-season crop into the same field.
